utterance: Hi Daniel, I'm the GP seeing you today. I understand your back has been very painful and you'd like an MRI. Can you tell me what you lifted, when this happened, and how the pain has changed since then?
reply: I was lifting a big pot plant in the garden on Saturday, felt a twinge, and then woke up Sunday and could barely get out of bed. I figured I'd need an MRI to see what is going on, because the pain is low down on the left side of my back and sometimes goes into my left buttock. It gets worse when I bend or get out of a chair and is worse by the evening, though it feels a bit better when I am lying still with a heat pack.

utterance: I'm going to check for any warning signs first. Have you had difficulty starting or passing urine, loss of bladder or bowel control, or numbness around your genitals, bottom or inner thighs? Have you noticed weakness in either leg or difficulty walking?
reply: My passing urine is all normal and I haven't had any loss of bowel control or numbness around there. My legs feel completely normal and I haven't noticed any weakness or difficulty walking.

reply: Honestly, I've been reading about slipped discs and people needing surgery, and I just want to know what's going on.

utterance: That sounds worrying, especially with this much pain. I'll examine your back, how you walk and the nerves in your legs now, if that's okay. That will help us decide whether a scan would change the treatment.
reply: Okay, let's do the examination. Does this mean I still won't be getting an MRI today?

utterance: Based on what you've told me so far, an MRI probably won't be needed today, but I'll check the examination before deciding. Severe pain alone doesn't mean a slipped disc or a need for surgery. Scans often show normal age-related changes that aren't causing pain, and early scans don't usually improve recovery when there are no warning signs.
reply: That just feels a bit risky when I can barely move, but alright, let us go ahead with the examination then.

utterance: The examination is reassuring: the muscles on the left are tender and tight, but your leg strength, feeling and reflexes are normal, and there is no tenderness directly over the bones. This fits an acute mechanical back strain, without signs of a trapped nerve. An MRI or X-ray wouldn't change the treatment now, so I recommend neither today. That doesn't mean ignoring it: we'll treat the pain, review your recovery and reconsider investigations if anything changes or it isn't improving.
reply: That is a huge relief to hear it is not a trapped nerve. What should we do about the pain so I can actually start moving around again?

utterance: A short course of ibuprofen may help you move more comfortably. Take 400 mg with food up to three times a day when needed, for up to five days, using the lowest amount that helps and stopping sooner if you can. Don't combine it with other anti-inflammatory painkillers such as naproxen or diclofenac. Stop and seek medical advice if it causes stomach pain; seek urgent help for black stools, vomiting blood, wheezing or swelling, or markedly reduced urine. Avoid it if you're dehydrated. Paracetamol alone often doesn't help much with this type of pain, and I wouldn't recommend strong opioid painkillers.
reply: I will take the ibuprofen as you suggested, and hopefully that gets me moving a bit better.

awards.label: Ibuprofen 400 mg orally three times daily with food, short course

utterance: Keep gently active rather than resting in bed or on the couch all day. Try short, frequent walks and gradually return to normal activities as comfortable; some soreness with movement doesn't necessarily mean damage. Avoid heavy lifting and repeated bending or twisting for now. At work, alternate sitting and standing, take regular movement breaks and use a supported chair rather than working lying on the couch. A wrapped heat pack for 15–20 minutes can help; avoid burns or falling asleep on it. Most episodes improve substantially over the next couple of weeks, although full recovery can take four to six weeks.
reply: Alright, I will try to keep moving and use the heat pack, but I will make sure I come back if things do not start improving.

utterance: Let's book a review in a week to check your pain, movement and work situation, sooner if the pain is getting worse or the medicine isn't helping. If you're not making progress over the next couple of weeks, physiotherapy can help with a gradual exercise programme. Persistent symptoms after four to six weeks would need reassessment, with imaging considered if the findings suggest it would change treatment. Would you like a work certificate for temporarily modified duties?
reply: A work certificate would actually be really helpful for the next few days while I sort this out.

utterance: I can provide a certificate recommending modified duties for the next three days, with regular movement breaks and no lifting, then review if you need longer. One important safety point: go straight to an emergency department if you become unable to pass urine, lose control of your bladder or bowels, develop numbness around your genitals or bottom, or new leg weakness. These can signal rare but serious pressure on the nerves. Seek urgent same-day care for fever, feeling very unwell, or new severe constant pain, especially at night. Could you tell me the main warning signs you would seek emergency help for?
reply: I need to go straight to the emergency department if I become unable to pass urine, lose control of my bladder or bowels, develop numbness around my genitals or bottom, or get new leg weakness.

utterance: Exactly. Those aren't present now, which is reassuring. We'll focus on getting you moving comfortably and review in a week rather than leaving you to manage this alone.
reply: Thank you, I appreciate you taking the time to explain it all properly. I will head home, take the ibuprofen with food, and try to get a bit of walking in.

awards.label: Correct diagnosis: Acute non-specific low back pain
Can't-miss diagnosis considered: Cauda equina syndrome
